title: Starting weights that keep the signal
objectives: Derive the weight scale that keeps activation variance steady through a layer.

screens.title: A signal that survives ten layers
screens.prose: Ten linear layers, each 100 wide, are fed 1,000 rows of standard normal inputs. Every weight is drawn with the same sd. Slide the weight sd and watch the sd of each layer's outputs (log scale).

state.caption: Weight sd 0.05: the sd after layer 10 is 1.0e-03

screens.question: Which weight sd keeps the outputs near sd 1 all the way down?

hints.text: Too big and the sd grows every layer; too small and it shrinks.
Look for the setting whose line stays flat.
At 0.1 the line hugs 1.

feedback.correct: 0.1: the sd after layer 10 is 1.06, against 1.1e+10 at sd 1 and 1e-10 at 0.01.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the flat line.

byKey.big: At sd 1 each layer multiplies the spread: 1.1e+10 after ten layers.
byKey.small: At 0.01 the signal shrinks tenfold a layer and is gone.
byKey.he: At 0.15 it still grows, slowly, layer after layer.

explain.text: At 0.1 the sd stays near 1 (1.06 at layer 10). Each layer multiplies the variance by the same factor, so only a factor of 1 keeps the signal.

canvas.caption: Weight sd 0.1: the sd after layer 10 is 1.06

screens.title: Why 0.1
screens.prose: Name it: for $z = \sum_{j=1}^{n} w_j x_j$ with independent, zero-mean weights and inputs, $\operatorname{Var}(z) = n\operatorname{Var}(w)\operatorname{Var}(x)$ (`random-vars` l10). Our layers have $n = 100$ inputs per unit.
screens.question: With weight sd 1, by what factor does each layer multiply the variance?

hints.text: $\operatorname{Var}(w) = 1^2 = 1$.
$n\operatorname{Var}(w) = 100 \times 1$.
The variance grows a hundredfold a layer.

feedback.correct: $100 \times 1 = 100$, so the sd grows tenfold a layer; sd $1/\sqrt{100} = 0.1$ makes the factor 1.

byKey.sd: Ten is the factor on the sd; the variance grows by its square, 100.
byKey.one: That is the factor at sd 0.1.

explain.text: $\operatorname{Var}(z) = 100 \times 1 \times \operatorname{Var}(x)$: a hundredfold a layer, $10^{20}$ after ten, so the sd reaches about $10^{10}$, as the chart showed. Weight sd $1/\sqrt n = 0.1$ keeps the factor at 1.

screens.title: One layer by hand
screens.prose: A layer has $n = 50$ inputs per unit, weights with variance 0.04 and inputs with variance 1, all independent with mean 0. A 20,000-draw simulation of our $n = 100$, sd 1 case (`default_rng(0)`) gave a variance of 101.0, against the formula's 100.
screens.question: What is the variance of one unit's pre-activation?

hints.text: Use $n\operatorname{Var}(w)\operatorname{Var}(x)$.
Times $\operatorname{Var}(x) = 1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the three factors.

byKey.sd: You used the weight sd, 0.2, in place of its variance, 0.04: $50 \times 0.2 = 10$.

explain.text: $50 \times 0.04 = 2$, so each such layer doubles the variance. To keep it, $\operatorname{Var}(w) = 1/50$, sd $1/\sqrt{50} \approx 0.141$.

screens.title: ReLU halves it
screens.prose: A ReLU zeroes every negative pre-activation. For a symmetric $z$, $E[\max(0, z)^2] = \tfrac12 E[z^2]$, so the next layer's pre-activation variance halves: with zero-mean weights, $\operatorname{Var}(z) = n\operatorname{Var}(w)E[x^2]$. **He initialisation** (He et al., 2015) doubles $\operatorname{Var}(w)$ to make up: sd $\sqrt{2/n}$.
screens.question: What is the He sd for $n = 100$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: That is $\sqrt 2$ times the LeCun sd of 0.1.

feedback.correct: $\sqrt{0.02} = 0.1414$; ReLU layers at that sd keep their sd near 1 (1.05 at layer 10), where sd 0.1 fades to 0.033.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the root of $2/n$.

byKey.lecun: That is $1/\sqrt n$, the right sd for linear or tanh layers, not ReLU.
byKey.var: That is the variance, $2/n$; take its root.
byKey.half: You halved the variance instead of doubling it.

explain.text: ReLU passes half the second moment on, so the weights carry twice as much: $\sqrt{2/100} = 0.1414$. A simulation of ten ReLU layers confirms it.

screens.title: The variance of a layer, derived
screens.prose: We derive $\operatorname{Var}(z) = n\operatorname{Var}(w)\operatorname{Var}(x)$ for $z = \sum_{j=1}^n w_j x_j$, with all $w_j$ and $x_j$ independent and of mean 0.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: $\operatorname{Var}(z) = \sum_{j} \operatorname{Var}(w_j x_j)$, since the terms are independent
$\operatorname{Var}(w_j x_j) = E[w_j^2 x_j^2] - (E[w_j x_j])^2$, the definition of variance
$E[w_j x_j] = E[w_j]E[x_j] = 0$, by independence and zero means
$E[w_j^2 x_j^2] = E[w_j^2]E[x_j^2] = \operatorname{Var}(w)\operatorname{Var}(x)$, by independence and zero means

lines.why: Variances add for a sum of independent terms, not for a product.
Independent terms add their variances once each: $n$, not $n^2$.

hints.text: Split the sum first.
Work out the mean and the second moment of one product.
Both need independence and zero means.

feedback.correct: Split by independence, then each product has mean 0 and second moment $\operatorname{Var}(w)\operatorname{Var}(x)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each line uses one fact.

byKey.x1: A product's variance is not the sum of the variances.
byKey.x2: Independent terms add their variances: $n$ copies, not $n^2$.

explain.text: Independence splits the variance of the sum into $n$ terms. Each product has mean 0 and second moment $E[w^2]E[x^2] = \operatorname{Var}(w)\operatorname{Var}(x)$, because the means are 0.

screens.title: Start every weight at 0?
screens.prose: Fay starts a 2-3-2 tanh net with every weight equal, so no unit gets a head start. The table shows the first layer after 100 steps when every weight began at 0.5.

state.caption: Every weight started at 0.5. Started at 0 instead, every weight stays at exactly 0.

screens.question: What went wrong?

options.text: Every hidden unit computes the same thing and gets the same gradient, so they stay identical
Nothing: equal starts are fair, and the units have spread out by step 100
options.why: Read the table: the three units have the same weights, 0.0186 and 1.2176.

options.text: Only the speed: equal starts take longer to spread
options.why: Identical units get identical gradients at every step, so they never spread.

options.text: The step size was too small to break the tie
options.why: No step size breaks it: the update is the same for every unit.

hints.text: Compare the three columns.
They are equal to every printed digit.
Same inputs, same weights, same gradient, at every step.

feedback.correct: The symmetry never breaks: three units that start equal stay equal, so the net has one unit's worth of power. From all zeros, nothing in the first layer moves at all.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the three units.

byKey.fine: That is the misconception. Equal starts make equal gradients, step after step.

explain.text: Random starts are what make units differ. Biases are another matter: they may start at 0, since the random weights already break the symmetry.

screens.title: Initialisation in code
screens.prose: Write `activation_sd_by_layer(depth, width, w_sd, act, seed)` as the starter's comment says, `lecun_sd(fan_in)` and `he_sd(fan_in)`, and `init_layer(fan_in, fan_out, act, seed)`, which draws $\mathbf{W}$ with He for `"relu"` and LeCun otherwise, and zero biases.
screens.question: Complete the four functions.

widget.how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests. Tests 1 to 3 compare `activation_sd_by_layer` exactly on seeds, and tests 4 and 5 check the two sds. Tests 6 and 7 check that a large `init_layer` draw has the right sd within 1%. Tests 8 and 9 check its shapes, zero biases and exact draw.

screens.title: A forecasting net that will not train
screens.prose: A desk's 8-layer forecasting net "will not train at any learning rate". Before touching the optimiser, you print each layer's output sd: 0.8 after layer 1, and each later layer's variance is a quarter of the one before.
screens.question: What is the output sd after layer 8? Give 6 decimal places.

hints.text: A quarter of the variance is half the sd.
Seven halvings take layer 1 to layer 8.

feedback.correct: $0.8 \times 0.5^7 = 0.006250$: seven layers after the first, each halving the sd.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Halve the sd once per layer after the first.

byKey.var: You applied a quarter to the sd; a quarter of the variance is half the sd.
byKey.eight: You halved eight times; layer 1 is already at 0.8, so seven halvings remain.

explain.text: Each layer halves the sd, so seven halvings give $0.8 \times 0.5^7 = 0.006250$: the last layers see almost no signal. Fix the initialisation (or add normalisation) before any learning-rate search.

ideas: For independent zero-mean weights and inputs, $\operatorname{Var}(z) = n\operatorname{Var}(w)\operatorname{Var}(x)$: at $n = 100$ and sd 1, a hundredfold a layer.

Weight sd $1/\sqrt n$ (LeCun) keeps the variance steady through linear layers, and through tanh layers working near $z = 0$; ReLU halves the second moment, so He uses $\sqrt{2/n}$, 0.141 at $n = 100$.
Equal starting weights never break their symmetry; biases may start at 0.

formula.name: Variance through a layer
formula.note: Independent, zero-mean weights and inputs; $n$ inputs per unit.

summary.trap: Starting every weight at the same value makes every unit the same, for ever.

quiz.prose: A ReLU layer has 50 inputs per unit.
quiz.question: What is its He weight sd?

byKey.lecun: That is $1/\sqrt{50}$, for linear or tanh layers.

quiz.question: Which can safely start at 0 in a dense layer?

options.text: The biases, since random weights already make the units differ
The weights, since the biases break the symmetry
options.why: Equal weights give equal units whatever the biases.

options.text: Both, as long as the learning rate is large
options.why: With both at 0 every unit is the same, and no rate fixes that.
Zero biases are standard; the random weights do the work.

feedback.correct: Biases at 0 are standard: the random weights break the symmetry.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What makes two units differ?

explain.text: Two units differ because their random weights differ. The biases then learn from different gradients, so starting them at 0 is fine.

quiz.prose: Ten linear layers of 100 inputs each start from weights with sd 0.2, fed inputs with sd 1.
quiz.question: By what factor does the variance grow across all ten layers?

feedback.correct: Each layer multiplies the variance by $100 \times 0.04 = 4$, so ten give $4^{10} = 1{,}048{,}576$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the factor per layer, then raise it to the tenth.

byKey.sd: That is the growth of the sd, $2^{10}$.
